3.4 — Projectile Damage, Tuning & Playtest

Your turret sees you, aims, and fires on a timer. And every bullet passes cleanly through your body, because the projectile is still just a picture. Today you close the loop — collision, damage, cleanup — and then you take control of the numbers that decide whether the encounter is tense or unfair.

The Problem: A Bullet With No Body ~15 min

Your goal: being shot should cost you health. Three things have to be true before it can. Something must give the bullet a shape. Something must notice that the shape met the player. And something must turn "met the player" into a change in a number. Go and find out which of the three is missing.

Select Assets/Prefabs/Turret_Projectile in the Project window and read its Inspector. Then select the Player and read its Inspector. Write down what each one has, and what the bullet is missing.

The rule from 2.1 still runs this project. Overlap messages only fire when the two objects both have a Collider2D and at least one of them also has a Rigidbody2D. That is why the projectile being "only a Transform and a Sprite Renderer" is fatal rather than cosmetic. It is also why a bullet may not need a body of its own: the Player has carried one since 2.2. Check that reasoning against the rule rather than assuming it.

Before you add anything, decide what kind of collider a bullet should have. Here are the honest options:

Setup for the bulletWhat the player feelsWhat firesWhat it costs
Collider with Is Trigger ticked The bullet passes into you and reports the hit without touching your movement. OnTriggerEnter2D You must give the bullet a collider and size it by hand — a default collider is sized from the sprite's import bounds, and this prefab is scaled. A pass-through bullet also cannot be blocked by a wall later without more work.
Solid collider (Is Trigger off) The bullet thuds into you. If your player's body is Dynamic, it can shove them. OnCollisionEnter2D Now the bullet is an obstacle. A fast, thin, solid collider moved by transform is exactly the tunnelling case from 2.2: at high speed it can skip past a thin target in one frame.
Trigger collider + a Rigidbody2D on the bullet Same as the trigger row, but the bullet is now under simulation. OnTriggerEnter2D (and a body you can steer) One more component per bullet, and a body that will obey gravity unless you change its Gravity Scale. Buy this only if your bullet needs physics — bouncing, drag, or collision with walls.

The second decision is whose script runs the check. Both answers are defendable:

Where the hit check livesWhat it looks likeWhen it winsWhat it costs
On Projectile.cs The bullet implements the callback, identifies what it hit, and asks that thing to take damage. Each hazard carries its own behaviour. A bullet that later becomes a fireball changes only its own file, and a hazard you delete takes its damage code with it. Every projectile needs a way to reach the health of whatever it hit.
On PlayerController.cs The player implements the callback and works out what just hit them. One file shows everything in the game that can hurt the player — which is where a shield or invulnerability power-up will eventually live. Every new hazard needs another branch in the player's file, and the player's script grows without limit.

Socratic: Choosing a Hit Model

  1. Which of the two scripts will you put the hit check in, and what does that choice cost you later when the game has arrows, boss lasers and a flamethrower?
  2. A bullet that stops the player dead like a brick wall would be miserable to play against. Which of the three bullet setups avoids that, and what is the exact checkbox responsible?
  3. The projectile prefab is tagged Enemy, just like the turret and the mobile enemy. Given that, how will a bullet ever know it hit the player — whose tag will you actually test, and on which object?
  4. Your player's health method from 2.2 takes a signed amount. What number do you pass to hurt them, and what would happen if you passed the positive value by mistake?
  5. What happens if you never call Destroy on the bullet? Describe the scene after a two-minute firefight and name the two systems that suffer first.
  6. A bullet in flight is a hazard even after it has left the turret's range. Is that correct behaviour for this game, or should a bullet stop mattering when the turret loses track of you? Argue it.
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Read each snippet for what it does in isolation, then work out how it maps onto your bullet. None of these is from a video game.

Example 1 — A hotel door that only answers to one credential:

// Everything that touches the reader arrives here; only one class of thing matters
if (other.CompareTag("Player")) { RegisterArrival(); }

Example 2 — A theme-park turnstile deducting ride credit:

// One method handles both directions: a negative amount spends, a positive one refunds
wallet.AdjustCredit(-rideCost);

Example 3 — A spent firework casing removing itself:

// The casing destroys itself so it can never be counted a second time
Destroy(gameObject);

Example 4 — A delivery driver reaching the person behind the door:

// Find the script on the thing you touched, then hand the problem to it
TicketHolder holder = other.GetComponent<TicketHolder>();
if (holder != null) { holder.Charge(2); }

Example 5 — A paintball vest (comment only):

// The vest is a sensor, not a wall. It exists to notice a hit that already
// happened and report it - it never pushes the player anywhere.

Predict Before Building

  1. Example 1 tests a tag; Example 4 fetches a script. Which one can tell you what kind of thing you hit, and which can tell you what that thing can do? Which do you need for damage?
  2. In Example 4, what happens on the next line if holder is null and you skip the guard? What does that error look like in the Console, and which line does it point at?
  3. Example 2 passes a negative number to mean "take". Your health method works the same way — so why is one signed method better than separate Heal and Hurt methods, and who will be calling it in Unit 5?
  4. Example 3 destroys gameObject. In your hit callback, gameObject and other.gameObject are two different objects. Which one is the bullet, and what would you accidentally destroy if you got it backwards?
  5. Example 5 says the vest never pushes the player. Which of the three bullet setups in the docs behaves like the vest, and which behaves like a wall?
Build Lab: Close the Loop ~25 min

Step 1 — give the bullet a shape. Open the Turret_Projectile prefab and add the collider you chose. Size it and check it against the sprite in the Scene view, remembering that the sprite is scaled and may sit on a child object. Set Is Trigger deliberately, not by default.

Architectural specification for Projectile.cs:

The damage knob:

  • What serialized field lets a designer decide how punishing one hit is? What type must it match to work with the health method you wrote in 2.2?
  • What default do you ship, given the player's starting health? Justify the ratio, not just the number.

The hit callback:

  • Which callback method receives the message — and does the name depend on whether you ticked Is Trigger? What is the parameter's type in each case?
  • How do you confirm you hit the player, and why is a tag check the right first filter rather than testing for a script straight away?
  • How do you get from the thing you collided with to the health method on PlayerController? Which GetComponent family call do you need — plain, InParent, or InChildren — and why?
  • What guard check protects you if the object you hit carries no PlayerController at all? What would happen without it?

Applying the damage:

  • Which method do you call, and what sign is the number you pass? Say out loud what a positive value would do instead.
  • What message do you print so you can watch the health change with no UI at all?

Cleanup:

  • Which object gets destroyed — the bullet or the player? What happens to the player's health if you get it wrong?
  • Where in the callback does the destroy line go: before or after the damage? What happens if the bullet survives a frame while still inside the player?
Do not reach for a manager. There is a StatManager.cs in Assets/Scripts. It is empty, it has no health in it, and it has no method to change anything. Health lives on PlayerController, where you put it in 2.2, and it stays there. You will meet the manager again in 5.3, when a scene change finally gives you a reason to move your stats.

Save, wire nothing new, and press Play. Stand in front of a turret and let it shoot you. Your health number should fall by exactly your damage knob, the bullet should vanish, and when health reaches zero your death rule from 2.2 should fire. If the Console is silent, check the collider before you check the code.

Bug Hunt: Silent Bullets

  1. Leave the prefab without a collider and fire at yourself. What does the Console show? Why is "no error at all" harder to debug than a crash?
  2. Now tick Is Trigger on the bullet but keep the callback you wrote for collisions. Does anything fire? Which pair of checkbox and method name must match?
  3. Comment out the Destroy line and stand in front of a turret for thirty seconds. Count the objects in the Hierarchy in play mode. Which two systems in your game slow down first?
  4. Remove the null guard before you call the health method, then shoot a wall or another bullet. What error appears, and which line points at it?
  5. Set your damage knob to match the player's full starting health. What is the encounter now — and why is a one-hit kill a design statement rather than a bug?
  6. Delete the tag check and let the bullet damage anything it touches. What would go wrong the day the player can shoot back, and why is a whitelist safer than a blacklist here?
Read the Docs: The Difficulty Knobs ~15 min

Difficulty is not a feeling, it is a small set of numbers you now own. There are no correct values in this project — only the ones you choose, and the player experience they produce. Fill in the right-hand column with your own numbers as you go.

Knob (and which script owns it)What it controlsLow value feels likeHigh value feels likeYour value
Detection range (TurretController) How much of the map is a danger zone. A close-quarters sentry you can walk around. A sniper that owns the open ground.
Fire cooldown (TurretController) The gap the player gets between shots. A bullet hose with no room to dodge. Long, tense waits between single shots.
Projectile speed (Projectile) How much reaction time the player has. Slow enough to walk around. Faster than a human can react.
Damage (Projectile) How punishing one mistake is, out of the player's total health. Chip damage they can ignore. A mistake that ends the run.
Architectural specification: build three turret personalities. The Overworld scene already contains two Turret instances — count them in the Hierarchy before you assume anything. If you want a third personality, duplicate one of the existing two (Ctrl+D); that gives you three. Do not duplicate both.
  • Which of the two existing turrets will keep its current numbers, and where in the scene does it sit?
  • For each personality you build, write down the four values before you type them, and say what player experience you are aiming at in one sentence.
  • Inspector values on an instance override the prefab's values. Where do your personality numbers live — on the prefab, or on the instance in the Overworld? What happens to the other instance if you edit the prefab instead?
  • Does a personality need to be a different prefab, or just a different set of numbers on an instance? What does your answer cost you when you want to reuse a personality in another scene?
Playtest ~20 min

Swap seats with a partner and run a silent playtest — the 2.4 rules: you watch, they play, nobody speaks. Watch for:

  • Did they notice the turret before it fired, or was the first hit a surprise?
  • Did they try to dodge the bullets, or just sprint through the damage?
  • Which of your turret personalities was most satisfying to evade — and which one made them stop trying?
  • Did they ever work out what the detection range was, or did it feel random to them?

Tinker: One Knob at a Time

  1. From your partner's feedback, change exactly one number. Retest with the same partner. Did the experience improve, and can you point at the moment it changed?
  2. Change two numbers at once and retest. Why can you no longer say which change did the work? Write the rule down in one sentence.
  3. Make a bullet that is slow but huge and deadly, and one that is fast but weak. Which reads as more fair to a player, and what does that tell you about reaction time as a design resource?
  4. Commit and push: "3.4: projectile damage + difficulty tuning".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain what the projectile prefab was missing and why no message ever fired
  • Defend your choice of trigger versus solid, and say which callback name each one requires
  • Explain how a bullet reaches the player's health method, and why the null guard matters
  • Explain why the damage amount is negative, and what a positive value would do
  • Name the four difficulty knobs, where each one lives, and your value for each
  • Say how many turrets the scene shipped with, and how many you added
  • Run a silent playtest and make one evidence-based change
  • Commit and push
